While the fear of child abduction by a stranger is understandable, statistics show it's extremely rare—estimated at roughly 1 in 700,000 to 1 in a million annually in the United States. In reality, most communities are filled with well-meaning adults who are willing to help a child who is lost, hurt, or scared.

As children in my city transition to walking or biking to school and around their neighborhoods independently—often between 3rd and 5th grade, and almost entirely by middle school—the greatest threat to their safety is not strangers, but automobile traffic.

If you're concerned about the welfare of children in America, the most impactful action you can take is to drive slower and remain undistracted. Adhering to lower speed limits in cities, such as the 20 mph standard proposed by global safety initiatives, directly saves lives. Please drive slower at all times, stay attentive, and share the road responsibly to keep our kids safe.

Keeps skin in the game for healthcare consumers but also allows the government to leverage its buying power to keep prices down and ensures everyone has some level of coverage. They provide better coverage, fewer denials and far better access to newer drugs.  John Q Public that has these plans, will not give them up willingly for a government run plan.

We're on Medicare and I am retired Navy using TriCare for Life.  When I look at what providers actually get paid on my EOB's, I know they are not recovering the cost of services.  The drug plan I get through TriCare for Life is good, as long as you don't mind being limited to OLD drugs and generics.  Something new that is better, is off limits with out pre-approval  it is on the formulary at all.

Medicare also only pays 80% of "allowed" charges.  It requires a supplement for the other 20% and it often costs more than your Part B premiums, for those in that plan.

Medicare Advantage plans should be eliminated.

Universal Healthcare is generally a failure worldwide.  Technically, everyone is covered.  Technically, good luck if you get a serious illness.  Look up cancer outcomes in the UK compared to the US.  I'd rather a visit to my doctor not be similar to going to the DMV.

Instead, they float this is a benefit that will not cost anyone anything - except maybe those evil rich people.   But European countries have higher levels of taxation at lower levels of income in order to pay for their state benefits.    

Nor do advocates want to address what is essentially rationing.    My doctor ordered a non-urgent echocardiogram at my last visit.    By the time I was back home, I had an email from a nearby hospital offering me dates to schedule, the earliest one week later.    Out of curiosity, I googled how long it would have taken me to get the same test through the British NIH.  The response was several weeks to months.    

The British Heart Foundation reports that as of March 2024, over 168,000 people were waiting for cardiac care, with 41% waiting more than 18 weeks for tests like echocardiograms

Until there is honesty about how such a system would be paid for and what health care consumers might have to give up, the supposed promise that it will be better, cheaper, and more easily accessible is just pie in the sky and shouldn't be taken seriously.... kind of like 'you can keep your doctor' and 'the average family will save $2500 per year'.

For our son, we prioritize the kind of education we received--a truly well-rounded, humanistic one.  If he wants to be a banker after that, more power to him.  If he wants to be a teacher or a clarinetist, we'll have money saved to help him.  That's what I work for. 

I guess I still have that immigrant mindset where you work for the next generation to do better, but I wonder why the complainers here aren't doing more to help set up their kids.  Either they're being disingenuous--the wealth transfer from the Boomers will be something, after all--or they're just kind of mean.  

I am reading 'Secondhand Time' by Svetlana Alexievich, which interviews people who lived through the fall of the Soviet Union. This morning I read a passage by an old woman who said her entire life had been suffering, and at every turn she was promised that a better life was coming.  It never did. 

Every day you have the choice to do something you don't hate is a gift.

Bravo to Macron, Starmer, Britain and France for setting an example of how to break down some of the artificial barriers others have formed between Nations and Peoples.
One surprising note: It is hard to believe that Brits previously found it so difficult to take a train through the chunnel to Bayeaux! A short day trip from London!
We certainly hope that France/Bayeaux will take this respite to construct a more suitable permanent home for the tapestry. Its current home and method of display are certainly in need of an update.

comments.body: There are works of art that are worth the trip to Europe by themselves.  This is one.  Luckily I saw many of the bucket list works before bullet proof glass.  I parked in front of the Scrovengi Chapel and strolled through the dusty front door and lounged on a bench for two hours drinking it in.  I stood feet from van Eyck's Canon vanderpeal in Bruges.  The Ghent Altarpiece up close.  The Isenheim Altarpiece too.  Alas, too late for the Pieta.

comments.name: Barbara Menard
comments.body:
What a delight it was to read this. My only remark in the negative is the ridiculous way that King Harold was referred to as “Godwinson“. He is either called Harold Godwinson, Harold, or King Harold. I just think it’s terribly funny and must be somebody’s (the authors’s?) desire to fit into the modern world in what he considers the correct way. But it is so completely silly and out of place. He was the king, for goodness sake. We know that Henry the eighth was actually Henry Tudor. But I have never heard him referred to as Tudor.

This is not something I am going on about in some sort of silly way. I think it is blatant evidence of something ridiculous that is going on. I think there is a modern unwillingness to accept old ways, perhaps old ways of respect or custom.
 I feel often that I am an observer now. I can make comment, but I observe as somebody from a past generation. We don’t generally curtsy or bow any longer, and we haven’t for a long time. But it seems we are being coerced into relinquishing some of our past linguistic mores by journalists or some such. Why, I wonder.

It's heartening to know that so many people are interested enough in works of art to beat a path to their door, to want to pore over them, to revel in them. It's a sign that in a world of so much horror, there's still some hope for civilization.

We all heard about the walkways collapse and many people know they were caused by a change made to the plans to make execution easier. At least in this case a change was requested by the builder and approved at a low level by the structural engineer who didn’t appreciate that this change entirely negated the integrity of his design. But fewer people know that the builder didn’t correct a buckled roof deck and ended up filling it with several feet of concrete instead of the 4” called for. Few people know that the strucural glass wall installed at the entry was not anchored at its base when the contractor deceptively installed anchor nuts that appeared to be threaded on anchor bolts  that actually.

Other times the overall system worked great, like after the Nothridge earthquake, when a failed weld was discovered (by an observant janitor!) that left the building within a few seconds of shaking long enough to collapse. The teams of engineers that travel to earthquakes to assess design codes immediately recognized that a catastrophe had been narrowly avoided in lots of similar buildings. comments.name: Jack Armstrong
comments.body:
Because of rapid development cycles, Nvidia's AI processors have a fairly short technological life.  It is hard to think of them as collateral for hundred billion dollar loans. 

When a company borrows money using GPUs (the computer chips used for AI) as collateral — basically a promise that the lender can seize and sell the GPUs if the loan isn't repaid — lenders typically only lend 50% to 70% of what the GPUs are worth today.

That gap exists as a safety cushion. But it's a thin one. If the GPUs lose value quickly, that cushion can disappear fast, leaving the lender exposed.

And GPUs do lose value quickly — especially older models, which can lose 30% to 40% of their worth in just the first year, as newer, faster chips come out and make them less desirable.

So if a borrower defaults on the loan, the lender may seize the GPUs only to find they're now worth less than what's still owed — leaving the lender stuck with a loss.

Aside from the intangible magic of the composer's actual handwriting, these original scores, for me, inspire awe at the labor required to produce a large score  (or, simply stay alive) in the pre-modern world. Every note, every dot, every letter, was written by hand.   In a room with no electric light, no indoor plumbing, no running water.   No car to drive to a rehearsal. No email to distribute the score.  No phone to talk with anyone about what you have written.  My god, how did they have time?

And yet, Mahler wrote mind-bending symphonies, in a matter weeks, with no way to hear what they actually sounded like until played.  Now, any yo yo (including me--I'm an avid amateur) can write music on a computer program, play it back one second later, email it to a colleague or performer, and edit it repeatedly, effortlessly.  With nary a thought about the demands of daily life: food, transport, poop.  

We take this all for granted because it's our life, and we can scarcely imagine it any other way.  But looking at a Mahler score reminds me that none of our modern comforts are essential.  It's Mahler that's essential, and he needed none of our tools to produce his astonishing music.

comments.name: DWS
comments.body:
I'm confused.

The new Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio test described in the article is only FDA approved for adult patients, aged 55 years and older, ALREADY exhibiting signs and symptoms of the disease. Why are people getting the Lumipulse test before showing cognitive decline?

Everyone with Alzheimer's has been shown to have amyloids in the brain during autopsies. BUT there also also many cognitively normal people with amyloids in their brains during autopsies. 

The only currently FDA approved Alzheimer's drug therapies are for Amyloid removal, but these are therapies with side effects. So the Lumipulse is useful as one screening tool if these therapies are being considered to treat measured cognitive decline. But without any measured cognitive decline, what is the point of taking the Lumipulse test? Again, there are plenty of autopsies of cognitively normal people that show amyloids.

comments.name: ArtM

Once again, and to be emphatic:
There is NO cure for Alzheimer’s.

There is NO definitive test for Alzheimer’s.

Alzheimer’s medication may or may not work. Alzheimer’s treatments are such that those  purporting to slow progression or more are simply educated guesses or cruel hoaxes. Progress cannot be measured because Alzheimer’s itself  plateaus, rapidly progresses, slows down, and defy whatever scientific method is applied. 
 
People say they want to “know” to settle their affairs. But this skips the part where there is no knowing because a supposedly positive result is inconclusive until it is not.

My wife and I experienced 3 out of 4 parents succumbing to Alzheimer’s. My dad died of other complications before it overcame him. He was the “fortunate “ one. None of them progressed the same. None of them had the same lifespan after doctors gave their diagnostic guesses. My MIL suffered for over 20 years. My mom and FIL far less, yet different. Doctors have no answer. We grew to understand and accept this. What do we do? We live our best lives as we are able. We are healthy and refuse to dwell on what might be. This can take over your life if allowed. 

This is not to say progress is not being made. It is. There is significant research into Alzheimer’s. But there is a huge difference between progress and cure. I’m not blaming doctors. A fair doctor will tell you the truth, no mumbo jumbo. Demand honesty.

Given how dry it was then and the subsequent heat waves since I would hazard to say that the forested areas of northern Italy that we passed through are a tinderbox just waiting for a spark.

When we flew back from Milan and passed over Switzerland -- there was hardly any snow cover even on the highest peaks.

Our local guides couldn't help but mention climate change and how its affecting Italy and all of Europe.

In the UK, it’s being heavily promoted across the media as a thrilling experience, even though it will be, at best, a 95% partial eclipse. I’m sure the journalists promoting it are well meaning, but as someone who experienced a total eclipse far out at sea in 1999, I can tell you that the difference between 100% and even 99% is quite literally night and day.

It’s like being in a completely dark room (or an airplane cabin) and someone lifts the blackout blind by just a sliver — suddenly, the room is flooded with light. That final 1% makes an extraordinary difference.

100% totality is the key. During the 1999 eclipse, I watched what I call the “black monster” advancing towards me across the ocean. As it arrived, the midday sky darkened, the stars appeared, and then came Bailey’s Beads. It was utterly astonishing and magnificent.

And then, just a few seconds after totality ended, the sky was flooded with light again and the magic was gone.

So while a 95% partial eclipse will undoubtedly be an impressive sight, it really isn’t the same experience as totality. Until you’ve witnessed that final fraction of a percent disappearing, it’s almost impossible to appreciate just how dramatic the difference is.

Last year I booked a holiday in southern Spain, for August 2027 to witness the “eclipse of the century” and I’m giddy at the thought of experiencing totality once again.  It really is the most awe-inspiring thing you will ever see.

comments.body: Just in time was doomed to failure.  Years ago Sears had catalogue business that was extremely successful.  One reason it worked so well is that Sears (and other large retailers like JC Penny and Bloomingdales and Macy's) placed orders with manufacturers of apparel months in advance and then stored those completed orders in warehouses to be shipped to the stores that needed additional goods, plus the catalog goods were always available too.  There was always tons of inventory and initial orders were very large.  The benefits to the retailers was better pricing. The factories were always busy and the consumer got their goods on time every time throughout the season (back to school, holiday, Christmas etc.) and prices were reasonable for consumers too.  Our family apparel business had 9 factories in New York and PA.  We did work for Sears, Penny's, Bloomies and the rest all year.  We were busy as beavers and made money for ourselves, our workers and everyone else too. We could never have survived "just in time".  Now, 60 years later business and everyone else is beginning to understand that inventory is an asset, not liability.  Even the Pentagon is figuring it out.

Developing a full-blown regional conservation and restoration program that includes monitoring firefly populations, identifying native species, working with farmers to reduce use of synthetic chemicals and restore habitat, educating visitors about firefly ecology, in addition to the very hard work of nursing insects through complex life cycles, is mind boggling.

My sympathies go out to everyone affected by this event. No mention here though of the depth of the epicentre.

In my experience, this is an important factor. As a general rule, deep quakes are felt over a wide area, but cause limited damage for their strength; shallow quakes are felt locally and do substantial damage, relatively.

An example: I clearly remember a quake of 7.0 in Ecuador that went on for ages. I went upstairs, came back down again and doors and furniture were still swinging gently. The epicentre was around 100 miles north of us and at a depth of over 70 miles. It was felt everywhere in the country and one wall toppling was the only damage reported. Meanwhile, there was a tremor of just 4 in Murcia, Spain around the same time that caused a load of damage, with a depth of 1 km.

The depth of this one is reported elsewhere at around 107 km (65 miles), so I am not surprised it was felt over a wide area. There will surely be some questions about the quality of the buildings though. No one should really be surprised at earthquakes to the west of the Andes, so it is sad that such damage occurred.

I'm no expert--

--but I'm struck by the novels composed by people who are not native Americans--

--but who set their tales in present day America.  

And I notice the striking contrast between their homelands (as depicted in their books)--

--so full of cultural riches (what with festivals and holidays and picturesque rituals handed down from wise and discerning ancestors)--

-and the comparative blankness of modern day America.  It's as if our country were a sort of canvas--

--on which these vivid memories are to be painted.  

I wonder if this Korean novel has something similar.  

Maybe not--

--because heaven knows! our country has snares and pitfalls enough even for native-born Americans.  And these snares and pitfalls provide material--

--for any number of exciting or disturbing novels--

--as we follow our hero or heroine through a veritable gallimaufry of perils.  Till we see him or her safely home--

--and lay down our book.  And sigh a long sigh of relief.  

"Well, thank goodness that's done!" 

In any case, New York Times--

--I was just wondering.  

Thanks.
